label.rationale: Nf7 and d8=Q+ force a rook-for-pawn exchange. Whether Black has a distinct positional plan beyond defence against d7 is unclear.
White can use the a-file or reinforce c6. The c6 pawn and Black's choice of knight or bishop coordination drive the continuations.
Both sides contest the c-file and delay or accelerate the d5 or g4 break. The tactical consequence of the alternatives is less clear.
Rb1 aims for the seventh, while e4 changes pawn structure before the invasion. The checking move alone does not establish a separate material tactic.
Castling and timing c5 change the c-file and central tension. White can keep the knight or trade on b5 without a clear separate tactical refutation in the nearest lines.
On a2 or a3 the queen has a direct repetition resource. The third root gives up the queen on b1 and the point of other structural play remains uncertain.
gxf5 takes the loose rook before it can return to e5 or c5. White can develop counterplay but an independent strategic reason for Black's choice is unclear.
The queen moves leave White time to arrange a rook and e4 or contest Black's queenside pawn advance and Nc5.
Neither side easily breaks the locked centre. White shifts pressure between the queen, knight and rook while Black reorganises the king.
The c-pawn can force the bishop exchange or even draw the rook onto c6. White's independent b-pawn advance gives other routes when Black stops c7.
f3 followed by e4 and Nd5 is a durable central plan, with g4 a separate knight challenge. The capture alternatives leave the tactical relevance uncertain.
Black reorganises bishop and rook to restrain g6. White reorganises the king and rook to attack b4 or unblock the g-pawn.

Kh1 takes the king off the g-file, changing whether the actual captures on g3 give check and forestalling a stronger forcing attack. Black keeps the knight outpost and pressure on the g-file independently.
dxc4 enables Qd4+ and Qxe4 against Bxc4. Delaying the central exchange or using the knight for it changes the pawn structure and placement on the queenside.
Qf2 allows Nd3 with a fork after Rxe5. The stronger queen moves instead differ in knight retreat and how to contend with the rook on the f-file.
Nxc5 followed by Rxa2 is a concrete counterattack involving the passed c-pawn. Kd3 and Nc4 are different from using the rook and king to support White's central pawns.
The leading queen moves change rook entry and White's g5 plan. Several tactical lines exist but the result turns on a diffuse continuation.
Rxa6 exchanges rooks into an enduring bishop and c-pawn placement. e4 instead builds the centre, and the immediate exchanges create no clear forcing gain.
Black can recapture on d5 in different ways, allowing Qh6 and the exact e6 sequence or Rd1 and Ng5. The ongoing centre break and fight over both files persist in the quieter alternatives.
Rook and queen manoeuvres on the f-file and the queenside pawn on b4 govern the replies. The exact tactical contribution remains uncertain.
Rxf8+ followed by f6+ wins decisive material. The alternative fxe6 immediately permits an unstoppable promotion, and the lines focus on concrete loss.
The a-pawn advance and its exchanges open different queenside files while h4-h5 fixes the other wing. Ba3+ alone does not establish an exact tactical penalty at this depth.
White's e5 exploits two capture routes while Bxe5 dxe5 can expose the king. The c-pawn break and play against Black's a-pawn supply alternatives.
The rook lift and Qg4 attack one wing while Black contests the c-file after the knight reroute. Whether any immediate tactic dominates is unclear.
Bxc6 forces a calculated sequence around the rooks on c6 and b6. King shelter and White's use of the a- and c-files influence the quieter moves.
Nxe6 is an inferior recapture compared with Rxd6, which keeps the rook active and attacks e6. The tied-down rook and f-pawn movement create separate pressure even after the local exchange.
The exact promotion choice determines the checking sequence and whether the defender can hold. Independent positional value beyond the two races is uncertain.

Bxa2 and Nxa2 are materially similar, but after the other root Qxc3 an intermezzo Nxf3+ changes the recapture. The near-term queenside passer and weakening of the dark squares also shape White's plan.
Ne3+ and Nd5+ change the king's route and whether the b4 pawn remains available. Advancing b5 or f6 creates different durable threats.
Capturing b5 permits cxb5 and the a-pawn race, while Re3+ changes the tempi and lets a different pawn advance. Black's queenside blockade and independent h-pawn counterplay matter.
The exchange on e5 allows Bd3 and Be4 with tactical threats down the g-file. The strong bishop placement and blocked queenside are distinct structural factors.
Nc4 creates forcing choices between Qxb4 and Nxc4 with captures on different wings. White's passed a-pawn and the fate of Black's b-pawn remain independent strategic factors.
A precise rook check buys time in the promotion race. Passing and blockading the b-, g- and h-pawns shape which approach gives the most practical resistance.
The Nf5 sacrifice can open the g-file and threaten h7. Black can defend by reorganising the queen and bishop and managing the h-pawn break.
